title: Burns: Airway, Rule of Nines, Fluids

questions.stem: Which findings suggest inhalation injury in a burned client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Soot around the mouth or nose
Red skin on one forearm with no blisters

questions.explanation: A, B, C, and D are correct: soot, singed nose hairs, a hoarse voice, stridor, and face and neck burns suggest inhalation injury. E is a superficial burn away from the airway.

questions.stem: A client with carbon monoxide exposure has a pulse oximeter reading of 99%. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Remove oxygen; the reading is normal
Give 100% oxygen; the pulse oximeter can read falsely normal
Recheck the reading in four hours
Give oxygen only if the reading drops below 90%

questions.explanation: B is correct: for carbon monoxide, give 100% oxygen, and remember the pulse oximeter can read falsely normal. A, C, and D trust a misleading reading.

questions.stem: In a burned client, what comes first?
questions.explanation: B is correct: the airway comes before the fluid math, because it can swell shut within hours. A, C, and D come after the airway.

questions.stem: Using the adult rule of nines, what percent is one whole leg?
questions.explanation: B is correct: each leg is 18%. A is the head or one arm. C and D are not single body parts in the rule of nines.

questions.stem: An adult has burns on the front of both legs and the front of the trunk. What percent is burned?
questions.explanation: B is correct: the front of each leg is half of 18, so 9 plus 9, plus 18 for the front of the trunk, is 36%. A, C, and D add the regions wrong.

questions.stem: Which burns are not counted when estimating the percent burned?

options.text: Superficial burns, red with no blisters

questions.explanation: A is correct: superficial burns, red with no blisters, aren't counted. B, C, and D are counted.

questions.stem: Using the classic Parkland formula, a 70 kg client has 40% burns. How much fluid goes in per hour during the first eight hours?
questions.explanation: B is correct: 4 x 70 x 40 is 11,200 mL; half is 5,600 mL over eight hours, or 700 mL an hour. A uses half again. C doubles it. D is the 24-hour total.

questions.stem: A client was burned at 2 p.m. and arrives at 4 p.m. with no fluids yet. The first half of the fluid goes in over how long?
questions.explanation: B is correct: the clock starts at the burn, not arrival, so the first half goes in over the remaining six hours, adjusted to urine output. A starts the clock at arrival. C is the second half. D is the whole day.

questions.stem: During burn fluid resuscitation in an adult, what urine output is the goal?

options.text: About 0.5 mL per kg per hour, or 30 to 50 mL an hour
About 5 mL per kg per hour

questions.explanation: A is correct: aim for urine of about 0.5 mL per kg per hour, 30 to 50 mL an hour in adults. B and D suggest too much fluid, which causes dangerous swelling. C suggests too little, which means shock.

questions.stem: How should the nurse estimate the burn size for a young child?

options.text: Use the adult rule of nines
Use the adult numbers and add 10%

questions.explanation: B is correct: children have a bigger head and smaller legs, so the adult numbers don't fit; use a child burn chart. A and D use adult numbers. C ignores other burns.
